newsitem.title: UK: UK poll battle heats up as ex-minister stands down.
newsitem.headline: UK poll battle heats up as ex-minister stands down.

text.p: A former Conservative minister embroiled in a row over influence-peddling stood down on Wednesday as a candidate for the May 1 election to try and bury a sleaze scandal that has dogged Prime Minister John Major.
But the opposition Labour party, warned the government would continue to be accused of sleaze unless other Conservative candidates stood down.

"It is now up to John Major to show some leadership at last and put the rest of his party in order and if he doesn't do that the issue will run right the way through to polling day," senior Labour MP Alistair Darling said.
Tim Smith, announcing his decision to stand down as candidate for the safe Conservative seat of Beaconsfield, said he had been driven out by an unjust media campaign.

"I very much regret that the action of the Guardian newspaper in support of the Labour party has made my course of action inevitable with its complete disregard of both parliamentary privilege and natural justice," Smith said.
Smith has admitted he failed to declare in the register of MPs' outside earnings cash payments he received from Mohammed Al-Fayed, owner of London's luxury Harrods store.

He resigned as a minister in October 1994 after a series of articles in the Guardian but stayed on as an MP, saying his failure to declare was mistaken but not illegal and claiming he was the victim of a media witch hunt.
A committee of MPs has been looking into claims that the money was paid to Smith and to former junior trade minister Neil Hamilton, to ask questions in parliament on Al-Fayed's behalf.
The committee has also been looking into charges another eight MPs received cash from a lobbyist.
But Major's decision to dismiss parliament last Friday, launching the longest campaign in 80 years, meant a report on these charges could not be published before the election.
Labour accused Major of deliberately closing parliament to cover up the sleaze scandal, charges Major bitterly rejected.

The row over sleaze put the Conservatives on the defensive again after a day which began with Labour fighting back against charges its policies would turn the clock back to the days of union strife before the Conservatives won power in 1979.

Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, goaded by miners whose strike almost brought down her government, and by print workers who clashed with police after being sacked by newspaper tycoon Rupert Murdoch, passed laws to slash union power.
Labour has said it wants to roll back her reforms by forcing employers to recognise unions where at least half the workforce wants to be represented by them.

The Conservatives, scenting a weakness in the campaign which has won Labour a 25 point lead in opinion polls, seized on the planned change. A concerted attack led by Major said Labour would destroy Britain's booming economy with new union strife.
Thatcher returned to the fray on Wednesday, making a high-profile visit to Conservative headquarters to rally troops and savage Blair.
"He (Blair) wants to introduce new legislation to enhance the powers of the bully-boy trade unions," Thatcher said.

But Blair, fighting after the most damaging salvo fired by the Conservatives so far in the campaign, told a news conference he would give "no favours" to unions -- the party's historical power base and still the main single source of party funds.
